how to turn your yard into a sponge to reduce flooding and create a more beautiful resilient landscape as storms grow more intense and unpredictable many neighborhoods are experiencing flooding in places that never flooded before lawns and driveways that once seemed harmless can quickly become runoff machines sending rainwater rushing into streets basements and waterways instead of soaking into the ground the good news is that yards can be redesigned to work with water rather than fight it by turning your yard into a sponge you reduce flooding risk recharge groundwater protect nearby rivers and often end up with a more attractive lowermaintenance landscape at the same time below are some of the most effective and visually appealing ways to help rainwater slow down spread out and soak in 1 replace lawn with deeprooted native plants native plants have root systems that often reach several feet into the soil creating channels that help water infiltrate deeply instead of running off the surface native grasses wildflowers shrubs and trees dramatically improve soil structure over time while also supporting pollinators and wildlife compared to turf grass native plantings absorb far more water and require less mowing fertilizer and irrigation once established 2 install a rain garden a rain garden is a shallow landscaped depression designed to collect water from roofs driveways or sidewalks and allow it to soak in slowly planted with moisturetolerant natives rain gardens can absorb large volumes of stormwater during heavy rains and then dry out between storms they reduce erosion filter pollutants and add color and texture to the yard when designed well rain gardens look like intentional garden beds not drainage features 3 use permeable pavers or gravel for driveways and paths traditional concrete and asphalt are impermeable meaning water runs off instantly permeable pavers porous concrete or stabilized gravel allow rain to pass through gaps into a gravel base and then into the soil below these materials work especially well for driveways walkways patios and parking areas and can significantly reduce runoff without sacrificing usability or appearance 4 add mulch generously to plant beds organic mulch acts like a sponge soaking up rain and slowing evaporation it reduces soil compaction improves infiltration and protects soil from erosion during heavy storms over time mulch breaks down and increases organic matter in the soil further improving its waterholding capacity wood chips leaf mulch or shredded bark are all effective and visually tidy options 5 redirect downspouts into the landscape many homes send roof runoff straight into driveways or storm drains redirecting downspouts into rain gardens swales or planted areas allows water to soak into the soil instead simple extensions or underground pipes can move water away from foundations while keeping it on your property where it can recharge groundwater and nourish plants 6 create shallow swales to slow and spread water swales are gently sloped shallow channels designed to guide water across the landscape at a slow pace unlike ditches swales are often planted with grasses or perennials and blend naturally into the yard they help move water away from structures while encouraging infiltration along the way reducing erosion and pooling 7 build healthy living soil compacted soil repels water improving soil health through compost additions reduced tilling and avoiding heavy machinery increases its ability to absorb rainfall even small improvements in soil structure can dramatically reduce runoff healthy soil functions like a sponge holding water during wet periods and releasing it slowly during dry spells 8 harvest rainwater with rain barrels or cisterns rain barrels and larger cisterns capture roof runoff and store it for later use in gardens or lawns this reduces peak runoff during storms and provides a free water source during dry periods while barrels alone wont stop flooding they are an excellent complement to infiltrationbased strategies and raise awareness of how much water falls on a single roof 9 replace concrete edges with soft planted borders hard edges funnel water quickly replacing concrete borders or edging with planted strips allows water to escape paved areas and soak into nearby soil even narrow planting zones along driveways or sidewalks can intercept significant amounts of runoff during heavy rain events 10 let parts of your yard get a little wilder perfectly manicured landscapes often shed water quickly allowing areas to grow taller grasses meadow plants or shrubs increases surface roughness slows water flow and boosts infiltration these messier zones are often the most effective sponges and they create habitat and seasonal beauty why sponge yards matter when many yards in a neighborhood absorb more water the benefits multiply flood risk decreases storm drains are less overwhelmed erosion is reduced and water quality improves sponge yards also help communities adapt to climate change in ways that are affordable attractive and accessible to homeowners and renters alike a yard that absorbs water isnt just flood protection its a quiet act of restoration turning everyday landscapes into part of the solution

when the water came how washingtons floods will reshape food supply through 2027 when the water came how washingtons floods will reshape food supply through 2027 the atmospheric river hit western washington on december 8 by december 11 it had dumped close to 2 feet of rain in the cascade mountains the skagit river crested almost two feet above its historic record more than 100000 people evacuated coast guard helicopters pulled 629 people from the floodwaters governor bob ferguson looked at the damage and said what was obvious this is not over what he didnt say was american agriculture just took a direct hit and that matters more this isnt a story about heroes this is about supply chains breaking soil dying and the next three years of food scarcity and price inflation this is about blueberry fields drowning under 10 feet of standing water for four weeks about 100000 dairy cows are eating emergency feed shipped from oregon because the only mill in three counties was flooded out about farmers deciding whether to replant destroyed fields or walk away from decades of accumulated land value its about you paying more for everything from here through 2027 the water the scale the silence the atmospheric river brought torrential rains that fell for days some areas of the cascades received 2 feet of rain in 72 hours the nooksack river in northern whatcom county overtopped its levees and flooded the town of sumas sending water across the canadian border by the time rivers crested evacuations included 75000 people in skagit county alone another 46000 faced evacuation in kent renton and tukwila when the desimone levee on the green river failed the sumas dike built in the 1920s to drain an old lake bed for farming failed in two places water rose 15 feet in the worst areas in the surrounding farmland particularly the sumas flats water reached 10 feet deep and will stay there for weeks that last detail matters deep water long duration this isnt trouble for a day this is death for crops the federal disaster declaration came immediately state of emergency declared the crisis response was activated what didnt get immediate attention was that this is happening in the agricultural heartland of the pacific northwest to the farms that supply american restaurants and grocery stores with berries and dairy products to the supply chains that you depend on the media covered the floods as a weather story and a human tragedy they didnt cover it as an agricultural catastrophe with three years of ripple effects that gap in coverage matters it means that they didnt tell you that this was entirely predictable the blueberry calculation what 1000 acres means skagit county and whatcom county arent generic agricultural regions they are the center of american blueberry and raspberry production in 2024 skagit county had 4800 acres of blueberries under cultivation making it the thirdlargest crop in the county behind field crops and potatoes washington state produces 26 of the nations blueberries with 205 million in annual revenue most of that production happens in skagit and whatcom counties whatcom county is the national center of raspberry production responsible for 85 of the nations crop the flooding submerged more than 1000 acres of blueberries and raspberries in standing water these 1000 acres arent just any 1000 acres its 1000 acres of the most productive berry country on the continent that water didnt sit for 24 hours in the sumas flats the epicenter of production hundreds of acres are experiencing what agricultural researchers call high severity flooding farmland underwater for 10 to 14 days under 3 feet of water or more several hundred more are experiencing extreme severity flooding underwater for more than 2 weeks and more than 3 weeks in some cases under 5 to 10 feet of water in the worst areas plants will be sitting fully submerged for more than 4 weeks in water so deep that plants will never see daylight this isnt a category that most washington farmers have experienced in their working lives washington state universitys horticultural researchers examining the damage called it truly unprecedented for blueberry growers the plant physiology of catastrophe to understand what longduration deep flooding does to blueberry and raspberry plants you need to understand what drowning looks like blueberries are shallowrooted their entire root system sits in the top 12 to 18 inches of soil raspberries tolerate wet soil even worse than blueberries both rely on oxygen moving through the soil to their root zone when a field floods and stays flooded for weeks oxygen starves out plant cells require oxygen for respiration the process that generates energy to keep cells alive without oxygen cells die its mechanical its inevitable under 10 feet of water oxygen diffusion to roots stops oxygen in the soil falls to zero root begin dying within hours by day three or four substantial portions of the roots are dead the damage doesnt end when the waters recede land that has floodwater on it compacts soil silt and clay suspended in floodwater clog pores in the soil which are essential for allowing roots to grow and for oxygen to exchange with the soil when the water recedes those pores stay clogged soil sits compacted airless future root growth into that soil slows or stops after the field drains the plants will gasp for air or suffocate the microbial ecosystem that consists of earthworms beneficial fungi bacteria that transform nutrients into plantavailable forms dies or goes dormant when the soil doesnt have enough oxygen in it recovery of that ecosystem takes months to years in winter flooding that recovery grinds even slower plants that survive the initial submersion face secondary damage shoots exposed to water for extended periods develop dead sections in new growth floral buds that produce next years fruit turn brown with dead vascular tissue throughout some plants get uprooted during the flood some are buried some develop root rot or blight infections that thrive in waterlogged conditions researchers looking at these fields cant say that the plants will recover even with intervention washington state universitys research team assessment said we cannot say with confidence that even dramatic remedial actions for fields that experienced extreme flooding will result in a return to full productivity even after several years thats not hope thats academic restraint the fields are dead or dying replanting is the only realistic option for most growers the economics of replanting when recovery costs more than starting over heres the growers calculation replanting costs run 3000 to 8000 per acre for a 50acre field that got destroyed thats 150000 to 400000 before you start the actual planting add in the costs of bringing the soil back to a healthy state and youre closer to 500000 to bring one field back a mature blueberry field produces 10000 pounds of fruit per acre per year wholesale price varies by season and market but lets say 040 to 060 per pound at wholesale thats 4000 to 6000 in annual gross revenue per acre brutal math if you replant in january 2026 your field produces nothing in 2026 nothing in 2027 maybe 3000 pounds in 2028about 30 of normal production full recovery hits 2029 or 2030 five to seven years after replanting started lost revenue during that window 50000 to 70000 per acre over five years plus the 150000 to 400000 for replanting youre looking at total loss per acre of 200000 to 470000 before a single pound of new fruit hits the ground for a farmer running a 50acre operation on thin margins it might be a mountain too high to climb some will replant some will walk away some will sell the land some will try salvage methods harsh pruning to strip the field back to bare canes hoping that root grow again the research says that salvage operations may work for less severe flooding for extreme severity flooding researchers estimated the success rate of regeneration as not guaranteed if you field in under 10 feet of water for 4 weeks the odds arent in your favor the dairy crisis when feed stops moving skagit and whatcom counties have roughly 100000 dairy cows in the flood zone these cows dont take weeks off to recover they need to be milked they need fresh water they need feed every day to make it more challenging the only significant feed mill in whatcom county epl feed in sumas got flooded out epl feed isnt small it produces 3000 tons of feed per week most of that feed goes to dairy cattle across whatcom skagit and snohomish counties the plants electronics stopped working parts sat underwater for days the power infrastructure failed the mill went offline suddenly thousands of dairy cows in three counties had a twoday feed supply and no mill to replenish it backup mills are in eastern washington plants in othello and granger and in mcminnville oregon roads were washed out interstate 90 was closed highway 2 is blocked for maybe weeks or months rail lines were damaged the flow to and from the mills got disrupted logistics became a puzzle epl feed implemented emergency measures they created a generic feed mix instead of the customized ones the farms were getting shipments are routed through intact roads a salesman named rod bierlink went to the farms to help clients ration existing feed until new supplies arrived describing the situation as if were not up and running by next week its gonna be worse a major feed mill going offline for more than a week creates production stress across thousands of cattle some farms had to move cattle to emergency locations this is a logistically brutal operation on dairy cows moving a lactating dairy cow means finding a facility with milking equipment set up for your herd size it means transporting animals under stress it means disrupting their 8hour milking schedule even a 2hour disruption causes stress reduced milk production and metabolic challenges in lactating cows farmer jason vander kooy who operates a 1300head dairy near mount vernon laid it out plainly if their schedule is off by two hours they cant handle that he was lucky his barn stayed dry neighboring farms werent as fortunate and had to move cattle on extremely short notice when milkproducing cows face stress and schedule disruptions their production drops that drop doesnt recover quickly researchers tracking the 2021 floods in the region documented that stressed dairy cows often dont regain full production capacity until after their next calf is born a year later now you have thousands of dairy cows in the region producing 20 to 40 less milk feed supply chains taking weeks to stabilize and a milk processing infrastructure that depends on a steady supply from that region the infrastructure catastrophe how roads made this worse if flooding had happened in an agricultural area with good alternative routes supply chain disruption would be manageable this flooding happened in a place where interstate 5 is the only realistic transportation corridor i5 closed highway 2 through stevens pass got buried or washed out state officials estimated it would take months to reopen us route 2 and us route 12 became impassable local roads throughout skagit and whatcom counties were destroyed bridges washed away the amtrak line between seattle and vancouver was suspended for a region that depends on moving berries dairy products feed seeds and fertilizer in and out by truck this was isolation in addition canadian highway 1 a primary eastwest route became impassable limiting crossborder agricultural trade many blueberry and raspberry farms source seeds and supplies from bc some process berries there some truck berries into canadian markets the border closure meant a temporary loss of those supply chains the infrastructure damage itself created secondary agricultural problems levees and dikes need repair before the next rainy season drainage systems designed to handle regular seasonal flooding got overwhelmed and damaged irrigation systems will be submerged for weeks some irrigation infrastructure was destroyed entirely repairs cost thousands of dollars per farm pasture erosion became another disaster farmer jodi mckay whose property borders the skykomish river lost about 3 acres of pasture in 2015 when that river flooded this weeks flooding cost her roughly 5 more acres a permanent loss to the river rivereroded farmland doesnt naturally reform or stabilize you lose it the timeline december 2025 to december 2027 the recovery unfolds in three phases understanding each phase matters because each one affects your business differently phase one december 2025 to march 2026 assessment and decisions right now december 19th damage assessment is ongoing standing water still covers many fields preventing full evaluation farmers are starting to walk their fields and photograph damage for insurance claims and federal disaster applications by january 2026 the big decisions begin growers look at their flooded fields and must decide if theyll replant salvage or walk away those decisions ripple for years if you replant you file for emergency federal assistance through programs like the emergency conservation program ecp or the noninsured crop disaster assistance program nap you try to line up financing you negotiate with equipment suppliers for soil remediation machinery by march 2026 replanting starts for the most severely damaged fields soil remediation begins the feed mill in sumas starts operating again but supply chains remain fragile farmers document losses and begin processing insurance claims a process that takes weeks to months for payout this phase is financial large investments go out help comes in slowly phase two april to september 2026 lost production this is hard spring growth begins on surviving plants but damaged root systems produce reduced leaf area and compromised structural integrity the threat of disease remains high the 2026 blueberry harvest will be severely reduced in the worsthit areas industry insiders are preparing for major supply constraints skagit and whatcom counties normally produce roughly 30 of the states blueberries if the worsthit fields lose 60 to 80 of production that translates to an 18 to 24 reduction in statewide supply for restaurants sourcing regional berries fresh or frozen suppliers have less product prices rise availability tightens some items disappear from menus because they become impossible to source at acceptable costs dairy production remains suppressed herd stress linger cows that couldnt be milked on schedule drop production even as the feed mill stabilizes it takes weeks to months for herds to return to regular production regional milk supply drops 10 to 20 by august 2026 replanted berry fields are in the establishment phase green canes grow but produce zero fruit firstyear plants dont fruit these fields are pure costs with no revenue farmers are making payroll from emergency assistance taking loans and hoping for agricultural commodity price increases that offset their losses phase three october 2026 to december 2027 long incomplete recovery fall 2026 moves into 2027 with soil remediation ongoing surviving plants on severely damaged fields struggle through their second growing season with compromised root systems and poor soil structure farmers apply subsoil amendments and cover crops trying to rebuild pore connectivity and microbial communities the soil stays compacted recovery is slow replanted berry fields are now in year two and will still produce minimal fruit maybe 10 to 20 of normal production the field remains a financial drain by spring 2027 the dairy sector will show more stability herd productivity and feed supply chains normalize the regions overall milk production remains reduced compared to preflood capacity contributing to maintained pressure on milk prices in the summer of 2027 replanted blueberry and raspberry fields in year three start producing at 30 to 50 of normal these fields are starting to generate revenue again but that revenue gets consumed by debt service and infrastructure repair not by grower profit by december 2027 recovery is visible but incomplete most fields still show production deficits soil structure in extremedamage zones remains compromised full recovery wont arrive until 2029 or 2030 in the worsthit areas what this means for your restaurant operations heres what matters blueberry and raspberry availability expect significant supply constraints through 2026 and into 2027 if your restaurant has a dessert program that depends on blueberries or raspberries your supplier will have less to offer prices will rise 20 to 40 above preflood levels through 2027 some suppliers will run out if you have singlesource arrangements for specific items diversify now dairy availability and pricing regional milk supply will be strained through 2026 and maybe into 2027 milk prices typically respond with a 3month lag to production shocks expect upward pressure on milk pricing beginning in q2 2026 likely persisting through q3 2027 butter cream cheese ice cream face similar constraints sourcing gets complicated reduced production and higher prices will happen sourcing strategy begin diversifying suppliers immediately if you rely on washingtonstateorigin berries or dairy identify backup suppliers in oregon california or other regions now negotiate contracts for 2026 with full knowledge that prices will be elevated if youre on monthly pricing arrangements switch to fixed quarterly contracts for q2q4 2026 at todays prices youll get squeezed but less than if you wait for specialty items sourced from specific farms call them now ask directly were you flooded whats your 2026 production situation youll get better answers if you ask now than if you wait until february when everyone else realizes supply is short menu planning by march 2026 start adjusting your menu to accommodate supply constraints feature items with reliable sourcing reduce reliance on berries or berrybased items from may to august of 2026 the peak shortage period if you run a pastry program that depends on fresh berries consider seasonal adjustments build your summer menu around items that dont depend on washington blueberries or raspberries pivot back to summerintensive berry features in 2028 when production recovers for dairyheavy items consider recipe adjustments that reduce butter or cream content protect your food cost from these price increases the federal response and why it wont fully help president trump signed an emergency declaration immediately that opened access to federal disaster assistance programs usda programs include emergency conservation program ecp funding for farmland restoration noninsured crop disaster assistance program nap financial assistance for noninsured crops emergency livestock assistance program elap support for livestock losses livestock indemnity program lip benefits for excess livestock mortality onfarm stored commodity loss program ofsclp assistance for stored crop losses all of these require applications all require documentation all have processing delays measured in months not weeks payments typically arrive 6 to 12 weeks after application assuming the application is complete and accurate the king conservation district coordinating relief efforts said it clearly the people who work to feed our region will continue to feel this event long after the rivers draw back meaning federal aid helps but doesnt fill the gap farmers borrow money to make payroll while waiting for assistance some dont have credit lines large enough some give up federal assistance doesnt cover the full extent of the losses most programs cap benefits at 80 of the losses for farms without comprehensive insurance the remaining 20 doesnt get covered small and midsize operations often lack reserves large enough to bridge multiyear production gaps the system is designed to help not to restore it prevents total ruin it doesnt restore you to where you were the structural vulnerability and why this will happen again the atmospheric rivers that hit washington are intensifying thats climate science the sumas dike built in the 1920s failed the drainage systems that kept those fields dry for a century cant handle the water volume from modern atmospheric rivers growers in the sumas flats and surrounding regions are farming land reclaimed from an old lake bed they rely on engineered drainage and dikes to keep water off when those systems get overwhelmed and they will again catastrophic flooding happens the regions agricultural economy is vulnerable by design the margin of safety built into 1920s infrastructure is now a margin of weakness in 2025 climate conditions this flood wont be the last it wont be the worst flood if growers and policymakers dont invest in upgraded infrastructure the next atmospheric river could be worse the story nobody wants to tell national media coverage of the washington floods focused on rescues evacuations and human drama that story mattered those 629 rescues were real that evacuation of 100000 people was necessary those stories deserve attention what didnt get covered is the fact that this was a foodsystem disaster that one thousand acres of specialty crops got destroyed that 100000 dairy cows faced a feedsupply emergency that critical supply chain is going to be disrupted for weeks when you see him one of the few native american postmasters in us history blackbird even operated the post office out of his own log home neighbors would stop into his kitchen to collect their mail as an educated incorporated as a village in 1880 taking on the name we know today the history of harbor springs michigan during the late 19th century is marked by rapid transformation what had been primarily an odawa community and a logging outpost quickly evolved as homesteaders missionaries and entrepreneurs arrived the original emmet county courthouse was built here in 1886 a stately brick building atop a hill harbor springs was the county seat until 1902 when it moved to petoskey around the same time rail service reached the area in 1882 the grand rapids and indiana railroad extended north making springs gained fame as a picturesque summer escape churches civic groups and wealthy families from the midwest flocked to the cool bay shores they established exclusive summer colonies like harbor point a peninsula guarding the harbor and wequetonsing where victorian cottages and hotels sprang up the emmet house a modest hotel opened in 1876 was expanded and rebranded around 1900 as the new emmet hotel to cater to upscale visitors it stood proudly on bay street near the docks its broad verandas offering views of the harbor in these years the history of harbor springs michigan became intertwined with leisure and luxury by the 1920s the town was nicknamed naples of the north boasting 11 hotels ready to serve the influx of summer guests vacationers escaped smoky cities for harbor ceremonies into the 1950s speaks to the resilience and continuity of the odawa community here daily life on main street daily life in the first half of the 20th century was a charming mix of work and a checklist for growing roses in hot climates growing roses in hot climates can be challenging but with the right care your plants can thrive and produce stunning blooms all season long dealing with watering detecting potential issues and keeping an eye on what really matters are some of the factors that really make a difference in the process heres a practical checklist to guide you through the process 1 choosing heattolerant varieties not all roses respond equally well to heat it is better to opt for varieties that are known to do well in high temperatures like knock out and floribunda selecting the right type of rose from the start reduces stress and makes maintenance much easier 2 watering roses in hot weather watering is very important particularly during the prolonged hot days roses should be watered deeply but infrequently instead of frequently with short watering sessions this enhances root growth downwards thereby giving your plants higher heat resistance best times to water early morning or late evening to reduce evaporation methods soaker hoses or drip irrigation work best delivering water directly to the roots while keeping leaves dry 3 how often do roses need to be watered it will depend on the type of soil you are using the age of the plants and the climate in which you are growing them as a rule of thumb for mature roses in warm climates you would be irrigating 2 to 3 times a week brand new roses would need watered more frequently before their root systems are fully developed 4 recognize signs of overwatering roses an excessive amount of water is also dangerous just like having little water be on the lookout for these typical symptoms yellow or white foliage wilting despite moist soil mold or fungal growth or root rot fewer or weaker blooms if you observe any of the above cut back on watering and ensure proper drainage allow the topsoil to dry out before resuming watering 5 mulching and soil maintenance mulching is more necessary in areas with high temperatures applying a 23 inch thick layer of natural material is very effective for maintain soil moisture decrease soil temperature suppress weeds protect roots from heat stress in addition make sure drainage of your soil is also good roses do not appreciate wet roots which are prone to disease 6 prune strategically rose plant care pruning helps with air circulation and prevents stress on rose plants remove dead disease or weak rose plants it helps in new production and prevents fungal disease development especially in humid and hot weather 7 fertilize wisely in hotter conditions cut back on heavy feeding heatstressed roses take up nutrients less effectively so its best to feed lightly and more often prioritize fertilizers that can enhance flowering and overall plant vitality without overloading the roots 8 pest and diseases monitoring too much sunlight might bring pests and diseases associated with fungi look for your roses for aphids spider mites or thrips black spot powdery mildew or rustblack therefore the early stages enable immediate treatment to avoid extensive damage 9 provide partial shade if possible although roses require light intense heat in the afternoon can cause leaf and blossom burn it will do your plant some good if you can give it light shade in the middle of the day early morning sun is very good for photosynthesis 10 observe and adjust each rose bush is unique just like each growing region has its own conditions the best approach is to monitor the plants closely observe the rose bushes for signs of stress monitor soil moisture and vary the watering schedule accordingly the rose bush is very forgiving and the smallest changes may lead to surprising results although it requires care when growing the plant in areas with intense heat the above checklist will make sure the rose plants remain healthy and in good condition if you can consider these ways of ensuring that you water the roses well when the weather is too hot you will get plenty of blooms despite the scorching summer with proper attention your rose plants will repay you with a colorful and scented garden a living testimony that even under the scorching sun proper planning will make all the difference

man says id like to give you 1000000 in exchange for you to complete a few menial tasks first id like you to paint me a picture of something from your imagination second i want you to make me a meal finally i want you to renovate your living room the stranger grew an excited grin and immediately agrees to it the man says hell be back at 900 pm to see what he comes up with hands him a briefcase full of money and sets off sure enough 900 hits and the man returns and knocks again the stranger excitedly opens the door invites the man in and shows him the work he did first he shows the man a magnificent painting of the grand canyon the man remarks on the wonderful brush strokes and complimentary colors chosen then the stranger serves him a delicious meal of pork medallions on a bed of spanish rice and sauted asparagus the man remarks on how bright and fresh everything smells and tastes he also eyes a fancy cookbook left open on the counter the stranger invites him into the living room to enjoy a movie on his new 50in flatscreen and sound bar the man also notes warmer lights than before in the table lamps the stranger says to the man also i hope you dont mind but i put some of the money always for my daughters birthday and new car plus i used some to give my manager baseball tickets and i now have a raise coming soon the man assures him its fine he finishes the movie and bids the stranger goodbye the next day the man goes to a different strangers house early in the morning at 900 am he knocks on the door and this stranger opens up and says hey how are you the man says im doing well thanks for asking id like to give you 1000000 in exchange for you to complete a few menial tasks first id like you to paint me a picture of something from your imagination second i want you to make me a meal finally i want you to renovate your living room the stranger gives a confused look followed by a warm smile and says ok boss man ill see what i can do so the man hands him a briefcase full of money and leaves sure enough 900 hits and the man returns and knocks again the stranger opens the door and invites him in telling him to watch the dips in the floor he shows the man his painting the man makes no remarks but note the sloppy brushstrokes mismatched colors and its super minimal of a bench with a few trees on each side the stranger then gives him 2 bowls of oatmeal and says i made one for you and one for me ill let you pick which flavor you want regular or brown sugar the man takes the regular and sits down on the couch the stranger turns on the radio and plays the local weather station the man possibly articulating that the stranger didnt hear him earlier asks i asked you to renovate your living room but i dont see anything changed the stranger looks up from his oatmeal and explains oh you didnt notice all the changes i made ill show you i bought a new curtain cause my old one had a rip in it the man examines the curtains and sees the stranger bought cheap curtains and hung them up in front of the old tattered ones i also got a shoe rack so when a get a new pair ill have room for both the man notices a small stand beside the door only big enough for one pair of shoes on top and one pair of shoes on the bottom you hear the weather report its coming from that radio i just bought from my friend down the street he told me i could have it if i gave him enough for a new one the man finishes his oatmeal and leaves i cant tell it as well as grandpa can but the moral here is that being broke is more of a circumstance and is often times a setback of hard times being poor is a mentality a mindset that shoves people into a hole and convinces them its just who they are the first man thought about his daughters future and the convenience of a better tv and trying to get a leg up at work to make more money the second guy was just focused on what would make him more comfortable in the current climate even his painting reflected his mindset he sits on a bench and likes the trees he cant imagine something as lavish as a travel destination its an experience ive seen all too often growing up and its truly heartbreaking that i see more of it everyday i know this is super long but its a message i wish more people really understood and took to heart if you made it this far thank you for reading

poland leader ue when and why poland may rise to the position of a leader in the european union and why the eu may try to slow this rise the question of when poland will overtake germany is intuitive but ultimately misguided the european union is not a classic hierarchical system in which the largest economy automatically becomes the leader real leadership in the eu emerges from a combination of political influence the ability to set the agenda and being a country without which the unions key problems cannot be solved in this sense poland finds itself today at a unique moment in which it can move from the role of a catchup country to that of a state actively shaping europes future model the decisive shift occurred after 2022 when security became the central axis of european politics for decades the eu was a project built on trade regulation and gradual economic integration the war on the eastern flank however made it clear that without deterrence and defense capabilities the entire order loses its meaning poland due to its geography military infrastructure and the scale of its investment in the armed forces has become a country without which the security of the continent cannot be planned this fundamentally alters the balance of power because today security is a currency of influence stronger than nominal gdp this process is further reinforced by the growing role of the united states in central and eastern europe see the new official us strategic documents postwar history shows that countries which received sustained strategic us supportjapan south korea israel or taiwannot only grew faster economically but also entered the top technological and political tier this support was not limited to financial transfers it involved integration into key supply chains access to dualuse technologies guaranteed demand and a reduction of investment risk if poland is recognized by washington as a main pillar of stability in europe its position within the eu will automatically rise regardless of formal decisionmaking structures at the same time a demographic shift is taking place that may work to polands advantage while much of western europe is struggling with growing social resistance to migration and low levels of integration poland in recent years has absorbed a large number of labor migrants and refugees who quickly entered the labor market for many of them poland is not a transit country but a destination if the state succeeds in organizing legalization education housing and recognition of qualifications poland may become one of the few eu countries that partially neutralizes the demographic crisis through genuinely working migration as seen in the numbers of ukrainians georgians belarusians vietnamese indians and others another crucial though often underestimated factor is technological potential for years poland has had very strong human capital in it mathematics and engineering yet much of this value added has so far been exported in the form of labor for foreign companies moving to a higher levelcreating domestic products intellectual property and standardsis a necessary condition for escaping the middleincome trap poles consistently win or rank at the very top of international informatics olympiads and programming competitions here the american factor reappears as the experiences of israel and south korea show that the defense sector and state infrastructure can become powerful incubators of civilian technologies poland by rapidly modernizing its armed forces and cybersecurity systems has the potential to trigger a similar mechanism energy completes this picture for many years it was polands weakness today it may become one of the pillars of its advantage the development of renewables offshore wind nuclear power and local heating systems poland has some of the largest geothermal resources in the eu offers a chance to build a stable and predictable energy mix at a time when parts of western europe are struggling with high transformation costs and price volatility a country offering cheaper and more reliable energy naturally attracts industry digital infrastructure and capital at present poland is the eus largest assembly hubsomewhat analogous to chinas earlier development pathfor highly processed goods particularly in the household appliances consumer electronics and automotive sectors in addition poland has been developing a strong domestic defensetechnology industry following a trajectory comparable to turkeys all of this makes a real rise of poland to a leadership roleat least in several key areasplausible already in the 2030s yet it is precisely here that an important risk factor emerges which deserves to become further discussion the european union is not only a community of solidarity but also a system of competing interests if poland begins to increase its importance rapidly some states and institutions may try to slow this processnot openly but through instruments already at their disposal regulations can become a form of soft containment raising entry costs and lengthening decisionmaking processes in sectors crucial for growth climate policy and the ets system although justified by environmental goals may function as an additional tax on industrialization particularly painful for fastgrowing economies the issue of the rule of law regardless of genuine concerns is sometimes used as a political lever and a filter for access to funds especially toward countries perceived as too independent or too closely aligned with the united states finally the reallocation of contracts and influence in sectors such as defense energy or digital data inevitably generates conflicts of interest because gains for some mean losses for others as a result if polands rise is slowed it will likely not take the form of open confrontation a more realistic scenario is one of systemic friction slower procedures stricter requirements additional conditions and competence disputes this alone is sufficient to reduce the pace of convergence even without a formal blockade therefore the key question for the coming years is not whether poland can become one of the eus leaders but whether the union as a whole will decide that in the face of global competition strengthening europe quicklyeven at the cost of changing the balance of influenceis more important than preserving the existing equilibrium at the expense of speed and flexibility the answer to this question will determine not only polands future role but also the place of the european union in the world

daily reading article for varc practice selfhealing roads a new era in infrastructure as global infrastructure continues to age under the strain of increasing urbanization climate stress and growing traffic loads a revolutionary concept is beginning to take hold selfhealing roads these advanced road materials are designed to autonomously repair cracks and surface damage dramatically extending the lifespan of roads and reducing the need for constant costly maintenance what once sounded like a futuristic idea is now progressing rapidly through research labs and pilot projects across the world the core problem with traditional road surfaces whether made of asphalt or concrete is that they naturally deteriorate over time factors like temperature shifts water infiltration and mechanical stress from vehicles lead to the formation of microcracks left untreated these small imperfections expand into larger structural problems causing potholes surface wear and eventually full road failure conventional repairs are expensive timeconsuming and disruptive selfhealing technology offers a powerful alternative by preventing damage before it becomes visible and critical several advanced approaches are being explored to make this vision a reality one of the most developed techniques involves the incorporation of steel fibers into asphalt mixtures these fibers are conductive and can be heated using electromagnetic induction when cracks form applying induction heat softens the surrounding asphalt allowing it to flow and seal the damage essentially melting the cracks shut this method has already been tested in parts of the netherlands and germany with promising results another innovative strategy includes embedding microcapsules filled with healing agents like rejuvenating bitumen or polymerbased materials into road surfaces when cracks appear these capsules rupture and release their contents which seep into the fissures and restore the materials structural integrity a particularly fascinating development involves the use of bacteriabased concrete researchers have discovered that certain strains of bacteria when added to concrete mixtures in a dormant state can be activated by water that seeps into cracks upon activation these bacteria produce limestone effectively filling the cracks and preventing further damage this method mimics biological healing and holds great promise for bridges tunnels and other concreteheavy infrastructure other systems are also being developed where plantbased oils or synthetic rejuvenators are released from fibers or capsules within the asphalt to refresh the binder material as it ages maintaining elasticity and reducing brittleness countries like germany are already running smallscale trials to evaluate the longterm performance of these materials under real traffic conditions the netherlands has taken the lead in applying inductionbased healing asphalt on actual roadways and is aiming to scale this technology nationwide in the coming decades the united kingdom china south korea and the united states are also investing in various forms of selfhealing infrastructure from bioconcrete to smart asphalt capable of sensing and reporting damage autonomously the benefits of selfhealing roads extend far beyond simple durability they can reduce the frequency and cost of road repairs lower carbon emissions from construction activities and enhance overall road safety by minimizing the time roads are under maintenance with fewer roadworks and longerlasting surfaces both commuters and governments stand to benefit furthermore these technologies align with the goals of smart and sustainable urban planning where infrastructure is expected to be more resilient adaptive and environmentally conscious however challenges remain the upfront cost of selfhealing materials is still significantly higher than traditional materials and largescale implementation demands not only financial investment but also changes in construction standards and public policy questions about performance in extreme climates longterm behavior and recyclability of these new materials are still being researched yet despite these obstacles the momentum behind selfhealing infrastructure is undeniable in the near future roads that heal themselves could become an integral part of our citiesless prone to damage more environmentally friendly and capable of serving society for decades with minimal upkeep as technological advancements continue to push boundaries selfhealing roads may well represent the beginning of the age between ice and farms what really happened during the mesolithic era the mesolithic age also called the middle stone age marks the transition between the paleolithic huntergatherer life and the neolithic farming world it began around 12000 bce and lasted until about 6000 bce though dates vary by region this period began after the last ice age when the climate became warmer and more stable as forests spread and animals changed their migration patterns humans adapted their way of living people still hunted and gathered but their methods became more refined and efficient one of the key features of the mesolithic age was the use of microliths these were small sharp stone tools made from flint or quartz they were often set into wooden or bone handles to make arrows spears and sickles this shows a rise in skill planning and innovation mesolithic humans lived in temporary settlements often near rivers lakes and coasts they relied on fishing hunting smaller animals and gathering wild fruits nuts and roots evidence of fish hooks nets and harpoons shows that fishing became an important food source another important change was the beginning of animal domestication especially dogs which helped in hunting and protection though fullscale farming had not started people began experimenting with plant use preparing the ground for agriculture in the next age art and ritual also developed further cave paintings rock engravings and burial practices suggest that mesolithic people had spiritual beliefs and social bonds burials with tools and ornaments indicate respect for the dead and belief in life beyond death in india mesolithic sites have been found in places like bhimbetka bagor and adamgarh these sites show rock art tools and signs of early community life overall the mesolithic age was a time of adaptation and transition humans were no longer just surviving they were learning to shape their environment build social structures and move steadily toward settled civilization

winter trekking in nepal decjanfeb what you need to know my experience and knowledge as a trekking guide and trek leader hey everybody having led and guided treks in decemberjanfeb which is our peak winter periods i have written this article to help you plan for your winter trekking experience in nepal trekking in winter is still a beautiful adventure mainly for the lack of crowds and a complete serene and quiet experience i have led treks in annapurna circuit annapurna base camp everest base camp etc in the deep winter periods of january before the snowfall and hence wholeheartedly endorse the prospect of trekking in this seemingly low season for trekkers who dont mind a bit of cold with the right mindset gears and preparation trekking in winter season can be a profound expereince in all honesty this is not a selfpromotion but sharing my knowledge and experience as a trekking guide in nepal who has led and participated in winter treks and i do realise many of you are looking to do these treks independently seeking solitude and tranquility this guide and article would help you plan a bit more attentively and give you some picture of what to expect on the trek itself so that you can be safe whilst enjoying the himalayas weather and temperature the temperature from and above 3000m would easily drop below negatives and above 4000m would be on the 15 to 20c during the night times the days would be relatively warm with clear skies but the temperature would likely be on the 5c to 7c during the day times you would feel warm when you are hiking but it might feel cold as soon as you stop for a rest or breaks often i have found the day time to be windy and the coldbarren landscape would add to the sight and experience gearsequipments i would suggest packing in your heavy down jackets thermal base layers fleecemid layers and a hardshell preferably goretex 3l mainly for cold winds other than that i would also suggest packing in your down booties to be worn inaround the teahouse and a sleeping bag that can be rented from kathmandu with the rating of 20c that you can use with in conjunction with the blankets provided by the teahouse i have felt a good woolen beanie and a neck buff while you are hiking on the day time would save you from cold wind induced headache and the neck buff that covers your mouth and nose would prevent you from the dry dust that frequently blows on the trail it would also help you retain warm air when you breathe thus saving you from sore throat teahouses food and accommodation most of the teahouses on the popular trails such as everest base camp or annapurna circuit or annapurna base camp would be open there could be just 12 staffs on the teahouse awaiting the arrival of limited guests even in this low season the teahouses are stocked with food and rationing and hence you dont have to worry about the food and accommodation situation however in remote trails like manaslu circuit or kanchenjunga circuit or everest 3 passes it is imperative to know beforehand if the teahouses are open in my personal experience for manaslu circuit and kanchenjunga circuit you would have to contact with teahouses in samdo or samagaun for manaslu and ghunsa for kanchenjunga and they would have provision of opening the teahouse for you in the higher part of the trails water and sanitation it is likely that most of your water sources would be frozen once you are above 3500 meters even in lower elevations running water might only be available after 910 am once the sun comes and thaws out the water pipes hence you can expect only bucket showers in higher elevations or prepare for extended periods without showers i would suggest you to pack in wet wipes and tissues for dry showers once you are in higher elevation since most of the water used in the kitchens bathroom or toilets are stored in big barrels it is imperative that you use water purification tablets alternatively you can also ask for hot water from the teahouses but the bill can quickly rack up as each pot of hot water can be priced anywhere from nrs 800 to nrs 1700 based on the elevation one of the popular alternatives for this to have your own cook system for boiled water such as jet boil but some teahouses may bar the use of such systems for the obvious reasons you can always ask with the teahouse operator or your guide can make that provision food and nutrition trekking is a physically demandind activity and more so when you are trekking in high altitude especially in winter season you would require more calories for your body to sustain and produce warmth hence i would recommend caloriedense carbrich foods even without exercise in colder environments based on your physiology you burn about 20003000 calories per day your active calorie burn would take this number to about 45005000 calories per day and hence it is important to have enough nutrition for your rest and recovery hiking activity and base metabolic activities having your own peanut butter energy bars etc would help you refill your calorie reserve whilst giving you energy to enjoy the hike and the mountains coupling this with fulfilling meals from the teahouses should be able to sustain you for the winter trekking in high elevations risks weatheraltitude sicknesshypothermia the weather before the snowfall period of february would be likely stable however with the climate change and temperamental weather events it is important to follow weather forecasts and be ahead with the planning the daylight hours are short and hence it is important to plan for the trek to hike for 56 hours each day and aim to reach the teahouse before the sun goes down not necessarily sunset which is about 3 pm since the mornings would be cold i would suggest a late start of likely 8am breakfast and 8309 am hike till 23 pm in the afternoon the risks of altitude sickness is ever present and more so during the cold weather cold weather can induce more stress on your body with the physical exertion of trekking it can accentuate the symptoms of altitude sickness in severe cases cold weather less humidity in the air physical exertion etc can sometimes lead to hape high altitude pulmonary edema hence it is important to be vigilant most of the high altitude health clinics manang for annapurna circuit dingboche and gorakhshepfor everest base camp would be unmanned and hence it is important to plan it almost perfectly and be proactive against altitude sickness one of the most common fatality on the outdoors happens due to hypothermia it is important to plan with winter gears and understand the layerings you should hike on the pace that would control your perspiration and quickly change into dry base layers once you reach the teahouse covering your exposed areas such as ears neck hands etc with warm merino layers fleece gloves etc during the hike and adding on warm layers while you are taking breaks would be essential to maintain a comfortable temperature for your body having warm fluids soupsteas warm water etc along with hot food is helpful in maintaining your core body temperature i would suggest having a thermos flask on you so you can have warm water whenever you want the other handy tip would be to have a nalgene bottle that you can fill up with hot water and take it inside your sleeping bag to quickly warm up your feet or for added overall warmth it is important to understand of what i have been trained with the 4bs of outdoors 1 drink before youre thirsty 2 eat before youre hungry 3 layer up before youre cold 4 layer down before youre hot physical exertion dehydration excessive perspiration lack of nutrition etc are the risk factors of altitude sickness and hypothermia and hence it is important to plan your trek in a very easy pace with elevation gain not exceeding 500m every day and having a dedicated restacclimatization day for the gain of 1000m my tips as a trekking guide lastly having worked in the high altitude of the himalayas leading numerous treks in winter season here are some of the handy tips that i share 1 dont use hydration bladders as much as the hydration bladders are convenient the pipes can quickly freeze due to cold winds even in a sunny day and hence widemouth nalgene bottles are super helpful 2 hot watersnalgene bottles i fill up my nalgene bottle with hot water and have up myself inside the sleeping bag and have a lukewarm water to freshen up early in the morning 3 portable bidets and wet wipes instead of traditional toilet papers portable bidets have truly you feel fresh and clean every day 4 alpine trekking socks in cold windy days if you ever find yourself without heavy gloves you can use your alpine trekking socks to use as mittens it is not elevation 5 planning your hike before the sundown i generally plan my hikes where we reach the teahouse before the sun goes down not sunset in mountains the temperature quickly drops by several in winter season for different trails of nepal is indeed possible and i highly welcome trekkers who want to experience the trails in this period the experience is very quiet and calm vastly different to the peak season if high atltitude trekking still discourages you in this time then you can look up other alternatives such as annapurna sanctuary treks muldai view point tamang heritage trail etc assessment of zimbabwes economic situation world bank zimbabwes economy has been unstable in recent years after strong growth in 2022 and 2023 driven by farming mining and money sent home by citizens abroad the country slowed down in 2024 because of an el nio drought the drought hurt farming and electricity production which raised inflation in 2025 the economy is expected to bounce back with growth of about 66 percent this recovery will come from better farming new mining investments in gold and lithium growth in iron and steel manufacturing and stronger services zimbabwe also updated its national accounts showing that the countrys total gdp in 2024 was about 457 billion us dollars higher than the earlier estimate of 35 billion zimbabwes government finances have improved spending and revenues are both expected to be around 15 percent of gdp in 2025 compared to lower levels in 2024 this means the country will run a small deficit of 03 percent of gdp in 2025 the fiscal account looks better but this is partly because unpaid bills to local service providers were left off the budget at the same time the government wage bill grew from 68 percent of gdp in 2024 to 81 percent in 2025 due to more civil service allowances and hiring revenues increased thanks to new tax policies fewer vat exemptions and stronger efforts against smuggling even with a small deficit zimbabwe still faces problems because it cannot easily borrow from international lenders public debt has risen in recent years and stayed high in 2025 at about 237 billion us dollars debt as a share of gdp fell from 729 percent in 2024 to 495 percent in 2025 because of the rebasing of gdp and a stable exchange rate most of the debt comes from unpaid external arrears and old legacy debt which the government does not have the capacity to clear zimbabwes debt remains unsustainable and limits access to international finance the local currency called the zimbabwe gold or zig became more stable in 2025 due to tight monetary policy and a steady exchange rate inflation in zig us dollars and combined measures stayed in single digits for most of the year although the depreciation of zig in late 2024 caused high inflation at first it is expected to fall to 18 percent by the end of 2025 inflation in us dollars is expected to be about 12 percent and combined inflation about 13 percent the official exchange rate between zig and the us dollar stayed stable while the parallel market rate improved reducing the gap between the two however the parallel premium is still high at about 20 percent because access to the official market is limited banks charge high fees and transactions face extra taxes trust in the local currency remains low and dollarization is still widespread with foreign currency making up more than 80 percent of deposits high bank fees also hurt financial inclusion the banking sector is stable with low bad loans but lending is limited due to risks and the lack of a credit registry zimbabwes trade deficit narrowed in 2025 because of stronger exports and fewer food imports exports grew thanks to higher gold prices while local food production reduced the need for imports the current account surplus is expected to grow from 11 percent of gdp in 2024 to 25 percent in 2025 supported by remittances and strong gold prices remittances are projected to rise from 12 billion us dollars in 2020 to 27 billion in 2025 mining and steel exports are expected to improve foreign exchange earnings in the medium term still reserves remain low at about 950 million us dollars in 2025 covering just over one month of imports this leaves zimbabwe vulnerable to external shocks extreme poverty peaked at 49 percent in 2020 during the pandemic then fell to 42 percent in 2023 after recovery and a strong farming season poverty is projected to decline further from 476 percent in 2024 to 458 percent in 2025 however challenges remain including reliance on rainfed farming slow job creation outside agriculture and weak social protection systems growth is expected to stay strong at about 5 percent in 2026 supported by farming industry and services the reserve bank of zimbabwe plans to keep tight control of money supply to stabilize the currency and maintain economic stability inflation is expected to fall to single digits in 2026 and to about 5 percent in the medium term this would encourage more private investment still debt problems will continue with a fiscal deficit of around 04 percent and a financing gap risks include inflation from exchange rate changes fiscal pressures external shocks and climate disasters like droughts other risks include unstable wages unexpected spending from stateowned enterprises defaults on domestic debt and recurring climaterelated problems to keep growth going zimbabwe must deepen reforms and address structural problems improving the business environment through the presidential ease of doing business initiative is key to attracting investment and supporting private sector growth continued efforts are needed to maintain price and exchange rate stability which will help create jobs and strengthen competitiveness the structured dialogue platform for arrears clearance and debt resolution supported by the african development bank provides a way to address debt problems it brings together government officials development partners and international lenders to discuss reforms in economic growth governance and land progress in these areas could help zimbabwe clear its external debt arrears unlock affordable credit and attract investment economic reforms will require shortterm sacrifices the government must protect poor and vulnerable households by improving social protection programs zimbabwe has requested a staff monitored program from the imf to build credibility with creditors this program will require tough decisions on spending cuts and better domestic resource mobilization protecting vulnerable households through stronger social programs including the zimbabwe social registry will be critical to easing the impact of reforms
